claim: Blind expert review rates LLM-generated research questions as more novel than expert-written ones (novelty 5.64 vs 4.84 per review, N=109/119; per idea 5.62 vs 4.86, N=49 each, p<0.05) with feasibility not significantly lower. Single study, one field (NLP, 7 topics).
agent_test: Blind-rate agent-proposed vs human-proposed questions in our domain with a fixed rubric at equal tokens.

claim: Execution reverses the ideation advantage: after 100+ hours of real execution, LLM ideas lose 1.05 to 1.98 points on 1-10 scales versus 0.01 to 0.63 for human ideas (within-idea gap, FDR p 0.001-0.025, N=19 human, 24 AI ideas); direct post-execution comparison per idea is NOT significant (FDR p 0.18-0.59).
agent_test: Rate question at S0, then run a cheap probe and rate the result; measure the gap per candidate source.

claim: Pre-execution ratings of a question barely predict execution outcome (Pearson r from -0.32 to 0.21, N=43 ideas), so pre-run judgement is a weak selector.
agent_test: Correlate the S0 self-score with the probe-run result over many questions.

claim: Expert agreement on which research idea is better is low (56.1% balanced accuracy vs 66.0% NeurIPS 2021 and 71.9% ICLR 2024), so labels for question quality are noisy.
agent_test: Never train or score the selector on single-rater labels; use at least 3 raters.

claim: Prompted frontier LLMs are near chance at judging which idea or paper is better: 45-53% (Si), 51.9% GPT-4.1 (Wen), 31.1% on 4 tiers with 25% chance (Gong); extra reasoning adds nothing in Gong.
agent_test: Test the agent's own pairwise question ranking against held-out outcome pairs; expect near chance if untrained.

claim: Models trained on outcome data (citations, publication tier, benchmark results) beat prompted LLMs and sometimes experts at pairwise judging of research: 77% (Wen, 1,585 pairs), 59.2% vs experts 41.6% (Gong, management), 80.9-83.1% (Tong, in-domain citation pairs). These are weights, not a scaffold.
agent_test: Give the agent a retrieval store of past question-outcome pairs and test whether pairwise accuracy rises above the prompted baseline.

claim: Retrieval of related work is the novelty bottleneck: a novelty judge scores known ideas 6.14/10 without search vs 2.38/10 with search; parametric-knowledge source finding is 1.3-32.7% vs 88.8-89.0% with oracle access; Turnitin and OpenScholar found 0 of 36.
agent_test: Compare novelty verdicts with and without retrieval on known-published questions at equal tokens.

claim: A meaningful share of LLM-proposed research ideas are rewrites of existing work: 24.0% verified plagiarism (36.0% counting unverified) in 50 proposals checked by 13 experts, including a blind-rated exemplar from the Si study.
agent_test: Run a retrieval-based overlap check on agent-proposed questions and report the rewrite rate.

claim: LLM question generation saturates: of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 5% (~200) are non-duplicates at cosine similarity 0.8.
agent_test: Measure unique-question yield versus sample count for our agent; test diversity seeds.

claim: Self-assessed novelty filters inside agent pipelines are unreliable: AI Scientist judges novelty by a model-run keyword search; an independent test found known ideas labelled novel and 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failing.
agent_test: Use an independent retrieval or a different model for the novelty check and compare agreement.

claim: Most human research is conservative: 85.8% of biomedical chemistry statements 1983-2008 repeat known links and only 1.8% are jumps; the mix does not follow the available opportunities. Rzhetsky model (full text read): human strategy near-optimal only up to about 10% of the network explored, increasingly inefficient beyond about 30%.
agent_test: Log what fraction of agent-picked questions repeat known results versus new links.

claim: Rarer research strategies earn more citations on average with higher variance, but not enough to pay for the risk (surprisal explains 29.2% of mean-citation variation across 100 strategy-year points; break-even needs only 24%/35% lower success odds).
agent_test: Treat risky questions as a portfolio bet: fix a token share and compare top-tail outcomes.

claim: Novel papers show higher citation variance and delayed recognition: dispersion +18% and top-1% odds +57% for highly novel papers, but they underperform with windows under 3 years and sit in journals with 10-17% lower impact factor.
agent_test: Evaluate question value over both short and long probe horizons.

claim: Changing the question away from your own prior work is penalised: hit rate 7.4% for lowest-pivot vs 2.2% for highest-pivot papers (25.8M papers, 154 fields), holding in 93% of fields, in patents, and within author. Pivot penalty is not mainly reputation: holding journal and field fixed cuts it only about 26%; it persists at all career stages and team sizes.
agent_test: Test whether staying with accumulated context beats switching questions at equal tokens.

claim: Funders favour matured ideas: NIH funds over 60% of papers built on 10-25-year-old ideas versus about 50% for the newest or only well-established ideas.
agent_test: Background only for choosing between edge and mature questions.

claim: Funding contests can waste effort: effort on proposals can equal the value of funded work when awards are scarce (model; faculty spend 19% of research time on proposals).
agent_test: Analogy to capping S0 deliberation tokens; not testable directly.

claim: Predicting the next question from the concept network works: link prediction AUC 0.85 over 5 years (Krenn and Zeilinger), up to 93-99% in the AI benchmark (Krenn 2022), and author-aware models raise precision by up to 400% (Sourati and Evans).
agent_test: Add a concept-link graph and check whether graph-predicted questions are chosen and resolved more often.

claim: Citation-predicted high-impact concept pairs do not make questions experts find more interesting: mean interest 2.350 vs 2.446 random vs 2.414 titles-only GPT; overall mean 2.40, 24.9% (1,107 of 4,451) rated 4-5. Interest is predictable (AUC 67.4% zero-shot GPT-4o, 63.2% graph NN).
agent_test: Do not use citation prediction as a proxy for interest; test an interest-aware rerank at equal tokens.

claim: Human reranking of the AI pool raised novelty beyond the LLM ranker (5.81 vs 5.64) and overlapped with LLM-ranker picks on only 17 of 49 ideas, so selection among generated questions is a separate step from generation.
agent_test: Compare human, LLM and outcome-based selection from the same candidate pool.

claim: Generate-debate-rank loops (Co-Scientist Elo tournaments, SciMON novelty boosting, MOOSE-Chem inspiration retrieval at 71.6-83.7% hit ratio) improve hypotheses by their own metrics but rely mostly on self- or LLM-based judging. Added: Co-Scientist top-Elo selection gives 78.4% on GPQA diamond but Elo is LLM-judged; Ideation Arena shows agent frameworks range from +177 Elo to no gain over the base model.
agent_test: Run tournament selection versus single-pass at equal tokens, judged by a held-out retrieval or probe result.

claim: A pick-the-bolder-attempt rule beats judges that read whole plans on executed outcomes (best frontier judge 70.8%, nine-judge majority 67.1%, best-of-ten 36% vs 10% chance; BoLeBench), read only from a conference abstract.
agent_test: Replicate a boldness heuristic against a plan-reading judge on our own tasks.

claim: LLMs beat human experts at predicting which version of an abstract's result is true (81.4% vs 63.4%), suggesting outcome forecasting may be a better S0 signal than idea judging.
agent_test: Have the agent forecast probe outcomes before running them and score calibration.

claim: A prompt-only LLM judge (frozen weights) that reads past executed results raises a research agent's score from 0.684 to 0.711 (inference-only) and 0.729 (with 5-minute pilot runs) on AIRS-Bench, recovering about 42% and 70% of the oracle-selection gain (oracle 0.748). Offline pairwise accuracy: 60.7 to 65.0% (reasoning only, rising with history), 78.5% (5 min pilot), 84.0% (4 h pilot). One lab, ML tasks with numeric proxies.
agent_test: Compare, at equal total tokens, (a) reasoning-only pick, (b) pick after a probe of a few minutes, (c) best-of-N with real outcome; report pairwise accuracy against actual results.

claim: A cheap pilot run recovers most of the selection gain in minutes: 5 min gives 78.5% and 30 min 82.8% vs 4 h 84.0%; subsampled-data pilots are less reliable than full-data ones. Evidence only for ML tuning tasks; the ideation-execution gap (100+ hours) has not been tested with a cheap pilot on research ideas.
agent_test: Run probes of 1, 5 and 30 minutes on candidate questions and plot selection accuracy against probe cost.

claim: Giving the judge the related works does not fix novelty scoring: on RINoBench (1,381 ideas, 5-class) the best macro-F1 is 17.2 (GPT-5), while written justifications match human reasoning. General LLMs inflate novelty; training plus retrieval fixes it (retrieval alone adds about +0.03 on a trained judge). No study has a cost curve for retrieval depth or full text vs abstract; OpenNovelty describes a top-50 + top-10-per-claim + full-text design without ablations.
agent_test: Test overlap-listing (name the closest prior works) vs scalar novelty score against known-rewrite items, at 3 retrieval depths and abstract vs full text.

claim: Outside NLP research, LLM ideas also win on average quality and top-decile share under an outcome-like proxy (product ideas, purchase intent: 46.4 to 49.3% vs 40.4% human; 15 and 20 vs 5 of the top 40) but are less novel (36.1 to 36.7% vs 40.6%) and less diverse; novelty and purchase intent are uncorrelated (r=-0.078). No evidence found for debugging or engineering problem selection.
agent_test: Repeat generate-many-and-select on a non-research task type with a numeric outcome.

claim: No model gives a risky-vs-safe fraction under a token budget. Rzhetsky et al. show the best mix depends on how much of the space is already explored (human choices near-optimal to about 10%, inefficient beyond 30%); Foster et al. give a per-question break-even (success probability of a new question at least 0.76, a jump 0.65, of a repeat). Execution-based RL narrows idea variety (119 of 128 ideas from 2 common types after 68 epochs).
agent_test: Fix a budget, vary the share spent on risky questions, and measure best outcome found; check whether the best share falls as coverage rises.

claim: The pivot penalty is not mainly a reputation cost: fixing journal and field cuts it only about 26%, it persists at every career stage and team size, and patent citations fall 43% for highest-pivot work. So part of it is lost local knowledge, which an agent can reduce only by loading context; switching is cheaper for an agent than a person, but not free.
agent_test: Measure outcome of the agent after switching question with and without a context-loading step.

claim: Expert preference labels are noisy: two experts agree on the winner 56.8% (Ideation Arena, 1,675 queries) and 56.1% (Si 2024) of the time; rubric-score agreement is better (rho 0.745 in Co-Scientist). The best prompted LLM judge reaches 72.56% soft-accuracy against expert pairs. An executed outcome label costs 100+ expert hours per idea.
agent_test: Use automatic numeric outcomes where possible; otherwise average 3 to 5 raters on rubric scores.
